entries.8d7eb49060ce5aa994715784dbc9b28c7d530092: <div sID="gen3148" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="23" osisID="Num.23" sID="Num.23"/> <div eID="gen3148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3149" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3150" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have Balak and Balaam busy at work to do Israel a mischief, and, for ought that appears, neither Moses nor the elders of Israel know any thing of the matter, nor are in a capacity to break the snare; but God, who keeps Israel, and neither slumbers nor sleeps, baffles the attempt, without any intercession or contrivance of theirs. Here is, I. The first attempt to curse Israel. 1. The preparation made for it by sacrifice, <reference osisRef="Num.23.1-Num.23.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. 2. The contrary instruction God gave Balaam, <reference osisRef="Num.23.4-Num.23.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. 3. The blessing Balaam was compelled to pronounce upon Israel, instead of a curse, <reference osisRef="Num.23.7-Num.23.10">ver. 7-10</reference>. 4. The great disappointment of Balak, <reference osisRef="Num.23.11-Num.23.12">ver. 11, 12</reference>. II. The second attempt, in the same manner made, and in the same manner frustrated, <reference osisRef="Num.23.13-Num.23.26">ver. 13-26</reference>. III. Preparations made for a third attempt (<reference osisRef="Num.23.27-Num.23.30">ver. 27-30</reference>), the issue of which we have in the next chapter.
entries.bccdeb357f78bbde29dedfc870fd77ed3ef9330d: <div eID="gen3150" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3149" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Balaam Constrained to Bless Israel; The Blessing Pronounced on Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1452.)</title> <div sID="gen3151" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And Balaam said unto Balak, Build me here seven altars, and prepare me here seven oxen and seven rams. 2 And Balak did as Balaam had spoken; and Balak and Balaam offered on <hi type="italic">every</hi> altar a bullock and a ram. 3 And Balaam said unto Balak, Stand by thy burnt offering, and I will go: peradventure the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will come to meet me: and whatsoever he showeth me I will tell thee. And he went to an high place. 4 And God met Balaam: and he said unto him, I have prepared seven altars, and I have offered upon <hi type="italic">every</hi> altar a bullock and a ram. 5 And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> put a word in Balaam's mouth, and said, Return unto Balak, and thus thou shalt speak. 6 And he returned unto him, and, lo, he stood by his burnt sacrifice, he, and all the princes of Moab. 7 And he took up his parable, and said, Balak the king of Moab hath brought me from Aram, out of the mountains of the east, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> Come, curse me Jacob, and come, defy Israel. 8 How shall I curse, whom God hath not cursed? or how shall I defy, <hi type="italic">whom</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath not defied? 9 For from the top of the rocks I see him, and from the hills I behold him: lo, the people shall dwell alone, and shall not be reckoned among the nations. 10 Who can count the dust of Jacob, and the number of the fourth <hi type="italic">part</hi> of Israel? Let me die the death of the righteous, and let my last end be like his! 11 And Balak said unto Balaam, What hast thou done unto me? I took thee to curse mine enemies, and, behold, thou hast blessed <hi type="italic">them</hi> altogether. 12 And he answered and said, Must I not take heed to speak that which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath put in my mouth? <div eID="gen3151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3152" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Great preparation made for the cursing of Israel. That which was aimed at was to engage the God of Israel to forsake them, and either to be on Moab's side or to stand neuter. O the sottishness of superstition, to imagine that God will be at men's beck! Balaam and Balak think to bribe him with altars and sacrifices, offered without any warrant or institution of his: as if he would <hi type="italic">eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats.</hi> Ridiculous nonsense, to think that these would please God, and gain his favour, when there could be in them no exercise either of faith or obedience! Yet, it should seem, they offered these sacrifices to the God of heaven the supreme <hi type="italic">Numen—Divinity,</hi> and not to any of their local deities. But the multiplying of altars was an instance of their degeneracy from the religion of their ancestors, and their apostasy to idolatry; for those that multiplied altars multiplied gods. <hi type="italic">Ephraim made many altars to sin,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.8.11">Hos. viii. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thus they liked not to retain God in their knowledge, but became vain in their imaginations;</hi> and yet presumptuously expected hereby to gain God over to them from Israel, who had his sanctuary among them, and his anointed altar. Observe here, 1. How very imperious Balaam was, proud to have the command of a king and to give law to princes. Such is the spirit of that wicked one who exalts himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped. With what authority does Balaam give orders! <hi type="italic">Build me here</hi> (in the place I have pitched upon) <hi type="italic">seven altars,</hi> of stone or turf. Thus he covers his malice against Israel with a show of devotion, but his sacrifice was an abomination, being brought with such a <hi type="italic">wicked mind,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.27">Prov. xxi. 27</reference>. That which he aimed at was not to honour God with the sacrifices of righteousness, but to enrich himself with the wages of unrighteousness. 2. How very obsequious Balak was. The altars were presently built, and the sacrifices prepared, the best of the sort, <hi type="italic">seven bullocks and seven rams.</hi> Balak makes no objection to the charge, nor does he snuff at it, or think it either a weariness or a disparagement to <hi type="italic">stand by his burnt-offering</hi> as Balaam ordered him. <div eID="gen3152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3153" type="x-p"/> II. The turning of the curse into a blessing, by the overruling power of God, in love to Israel, which is the account Moses gives of it, <reference osisRef="Deut.23.5">Deut. xxiii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen3153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3154" type="x-p"/> 1. God puts the blessing into the mouth of Balaam. While the sacrifices were burning, Balaam retired; he <hi type="italic">went solitary,</hi> into some dark grove on the top of the high place, <reference osisRef="Num.23.3">v. 3</reference>, marg. Thus much he knew, that solitude gives a good opportunity for communion with God; those that would meet with him must retire from the world, and the business and conversation of it, and love to be private, reckoning themselves never less alone than when alone, because the Father is with them. Enter therefore into thy closet, and shut the door, and be assured that God will meet thee if thou <hi type="italic">seek him in the due order.</hi> But Balaam retired with a peradventure only, having some thoughts that God might meet him; but being conscious to himself of guilt, and knowing that God had lately met him in anger, he had reason to speak doubtfully: <hi type="italic">Peradventure the Lord will come to meet me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.23.3">v. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">But let not such a man think that he shall receive any</hi> favour from God. Nay, it should seem, though he pretended to go and meet with God, he really designed to use enchantments; see <reference osisRef="Num.24.1">ch. xxiv. 1</reference>. But, whatever he intended. God designed to serve his own glory by him, and therefore <hi type="italic">met Balaam,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.23.4">v. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">What communion has light with darkness?</hi> No friendly communion, we may be sure. Balaam's way was still perverse, and God was still an adversary to him; but, Balak having chosen him for his oracle, God would constrain him to utter such a confession, to the honour of God and Israel, as should render those for ever inexcusable who should appear in arms against them. When Balaam was aware that God met him, probably by an angel, he boasted of his performances: <hi type="italic">I have prepared seven altars, and offered upon every altar a bullock and a ram.</hi> How had he done it? It cost him nothing; it was done at Balak's expense; yet, (1.) He boasts of it, as if he had done some mighty thing. The acts of devotion which are done in hypocrisy are commonly reflected upon with pride and vain glory. Thus the Pharisee went up to the temple to boast of his religion, <reference osisRef="Luke.18.11-Luke.18.12">Luke xviii. 11, 12</reference>. (2.) He insists upon it as a reason why God should gratify him in his desire to curse Israel, as if now he had made God his debtor, and might draw upon him for what he pleased. He thinks God is so much beholden to him for these sacrifices that the least he can do in recompense for them is to sacrifice his Israel to the malice of the king of Moab. Note, It is a common cheat that wicked people put upon themselves, to think that by the shows of piety they may prevail with God to countenance them, and connive at them, in their greatest immoralities, especially in persecution, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.5">Isa. lxvi. 5</reference>. However, thought the sacrifice was an abomination, God took the occasion of Balaam's expectation to <hi type="italic">put a word into his mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.23.5">v. 5</reference>); <hi type="italic">for the answer of the tongue if from the Lord,</hi> and thus he would show how much those are mistaken who say, <hi type="italic">With our tongue we will prevail, our lips are our own,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.12.4">Ps. xii. 4</reference>. He that made man's mouth knows how to manage it, and to serve his own purposes by it. This speaks terror to daring sinners, that <hi type="italic">set their mouth against the heavens. God can make their own tongues to fall upon them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.64.8">Ps. lxiv. 8</reference>. And it speaks comfort to God's witnesses, whom at any time he calls out to appear for him; if God put a word into the mouth of Balaam, who would have defied God and Israel, surely he will not be wanting to those who desire to glorify God and edify his people by their testimony, but it <hi type="italic">shall be given them in that same hour what they should speak.</hi> <div eID="gen3154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3155" type="x-p"/> 2. Balaam pronounces the blessing in the ears of Balak. He found him <hi type="italic">standing by his burnt-sacrifice</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.23.6">v. 6</reference>), closely attending it, and earnestly expecting the success. Those that would have an answer of peace from God must abide by the sacrifice, and <hi type="italic">attend on the Lord without distraction, not weary in well doing.</hi> Balaam, having fixed himself in the place appointed for his denouncing curses against Israel, which perhaps he had drawn up in form ready to deliver, takes up his parable, and it proves a blessing, <reference osisRef="Num.23.7">v. 7</reference>. He pronounces Israel safe and happy, and so blesses them. <div eID="gen3155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3156" type="x-p"/> (1.) He pronounces them safe, and out of the reach of his envenomed darts. [1.] He owns that the design was to curse them, that Balak sent for him out of his own country, and that he came, with that intent, <reference osisRef="Num.23.7">v. 7</reference>. The message sent to him was, <hi type="italic">Come, curse me Jacob, and come, defy Israel.</hi> Balak intended to make war upon them, and he would have Balaam to bless his arms, and to prophesy and pray for the ruin of Israel. [2.] He owns the design defeated, and his own inability to accomplish it. He could not so much as give them an ill word or an ill wish: <hi type="italic">How shall I curse those whom God has not cursed?</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.23.8">v. 8</reference>. Not that therefore he would not do it, but therefore he could not do it. This is a fair confession, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Of the weakness and impotency of his own magic skill, for which others valued him so much, and doubtless he valued himself no less. He was the most celebrated man of that profession, and yet owns himself baffled. God had warned the Israelites not to use divination (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.31">Lev. xix. 31</reference>), and this providence gave them a reason for that law, by showing them the weakness and folly of it. As they had seen the magicians of Egypt befooled, so, here, the great conjurer of the east. See <reference osisRef="Isa.47.12-Isa.47.14">Isa. xlvii. 12-14</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is a confession of the sovereignty and dominion of the divine power. He owns that he could do no more than God would suffer him to do, for God could overrule all his purposes, and turn his counsels headlong. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> It is a confession of the inviolable security of the people of God. Note, 1. God's Israel are owned and blessed of him. He has not cursed them, for they are delivered from the curse of the law; he has not defied them, nor rejected or abandoned them, though mean and vile. 2. Those that have the good-will of Heaven have the ill-will of hell; the serpent and this seed have an enmity to them. 3. Though the enemies of God's people may prevail far against them, yet they cannot curse them; that is, they cannot do them any real mischief, much less a ruining mischief, for they cannot <hi type="italic">separate them from the love of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.39">Rom. viii. 39</reference>. <div eID="gen3156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3157" type="x-p"/> (2.) He pronounces them happy in three things:— <div eID="gen3157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3158" type="x-p"/> [1.] Happy in their peculiarity, and distinction from the rest of the nations: <hi type="italic">From the top of the rock I see him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.23.9">v. 9</reference>. And it seems to have been a great surprise to him that whereas, it is probable, they were represented to him as a rude and disorderly rabble, that infested the countries round about in rambling parties, he was them a regular incorporated camp, in which appeared all the marks of discipline and good order; he saw them a people dwelling alone, and foresaw they would continue so, and their singularity would be their unspeakable honour. Persons of quality we call person of <hi type="italic">distinction;</hi> this was Israel's praise, though their enemies turned it to their reproach, that they differed from all the neighbouring nations, not only in their religion and sacred rites, but in their diet, and dress, and common usages, as a people called out of the world, and not to be conformed to it. They never lost their reputation till they <hi type="italic">mingled among the heathen,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.106.35">Ps. cvi. 35</reference>. Note, It is the duty and honour of those that are dedicated to God to be separated from the world, and not to walk according to the course and custom of it. Those who make conscience of peculiar duties may take the comfort of peculiar privileges, which it is probable Balaam has an eye to here. God's Israel shall not stand upon a level with other nations, but be dignified above them all, as a people near to God, and set apart for him. <div eID="gen3158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3159" type="x-p"/> [2.] Happy in their numbers, not so few and despicable as they were represented to him, but an innumerable company, which made them both honourable and formidable (<reference osisRef="Num.23.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Who can count the dust of Jacob?</hi> The number of the people was the thing that Balak was vexed at (<reference osisRef="Num.22.3">ch. xxii. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Moab was afraid of them, because they were many;</hi> and God does here by Balaam promote that fear and vexation, foretelling their further increase. Balak would have him see <hi type="italic">the utmost part of the people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.22.41">ch. xxii. 41</reference>), hoping the more he saw of them the more he would be exasperated against them, and throw about his curses with the more keenness and rage; but it proved quite contrary: instead of being angry at their numbers, he admired them. The better acquainted we are with God's people the better opinion we have of them. He takes notice of the number, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Of the <hi type="italic">dust of Jacob;</hi> that is, the people of Jacob, concerning whom it was foretold that they should be as the dust for number, <reference osisRef="Gen.28.14">Gen. xxviii. 14</reference>. Thus he owns the fulfilling of the promise made to the fathers, and expects that it should be yet further accomplished. Perhaps it was part of David's fault in numbering the people that he offered to count the dust of Jacob, which God had said should be innumerable. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Of the <hi type="italic">fourth part of Israel,</hi> alluding to the form of their camp, which was cast into four squadrons, under four standards. Note, God's Israel are a very great body, his spiritual Israel are so, and they will appear to be so when they shall all be gathered together unto him in the great day, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Rev. vii. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen3159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3160" type="x-p"/> [3.] Happy in their end: <hi type="italic">Let me die the death of the righteous</hi> Israelites, that are in covenant with God, and let my <hi type="italic">last end, or future state, be like theirs, or my recompence,</hi> namely, in the other world. Here, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is taken for granted that death is the end of all men; the righteous themselves must die: and it is good for us to think of this with application, as Balaam himself does here, speaking of his own death. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> he goes upon the supposition of the soul's immortality, and a different state on the other side death, to which this is a noble testimony, and an evidence of its being anciently known and believed. For how could the death of the righteous be more desirable than the death of the wicked upon any other account than as it involved happiness in another world, since in the manner and circumstances of dying we see <hi type="italic">all things come alike to all? Thirdly,</hi> He pronounces the righteous truly blessed, not only while they live, but when they die, which makes their death not only more desirable than the death of others, but even more desirable than life itself; for in that sense his wish may be taken. Not only, "When I do die, let me die the death of the righteous;" but, "I could even now be willing to die, on condition that I might <hi type="italic">die the death of the righteous,</hi> and reach my end this moment, provided it might be like his." Very near the place where Balaam now was, on one of the mountains of Moab, not long after this, Moses died, and to that perhaps God, who put this word into his mouth, designed it should have a reference, that by it Moses might be encouraged to go up and die such a death as Balaam himself wished to die. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> He shows his opinion of religion to be better than his resolution; there are many who desire to die the death of the righteous, but do not endeavour to live the life of the righteous. Gladly would they have their end like theirs, but not their way. They would be saints in heaven, but not saints on earth. This is the <hi type="italic">desire of the slothful, which kills him, because his hands refuse to labour.</hi> This of Balaam's is only a wish, not a prayer, and it is a vain wish, being only a wish for the end, without any care for the means. Thus far this blessing goes, even to death, and beyond it, as far as the last end. Now, <div eID="gen3160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3161" type="x-p"/> III. We are told, 1. How Balak fretted at it, <reference osisRef="Num.23.11">v. 11</reference>. He pretended to honour the Lord with his sacrifices, and to wait for the answer God would send him; and yet, when it did not prove according to his mind, he forgot God, and flew into a great passion against Balaam, as if it had been purely his doing: "<hi type="italic">What hast thou done unto me!</hi> How hast thou disappointed me!" Sometimes God makes the enemies of his church a vexation one to another, while he that sits in heaven laughs at them, and the efforts of their impotent malice. 2. How Balaam was forced to acquiesce in it. He submits because he cannot help it, and yet humours the thing with no small address, as if he had been peculiarly conscientious, answering Balak with the gravity of a prophet: <hi type="italic">Must I not take heed to speak that which the Lord has put in my mouth?</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.23.12">v. 12</reference>. Thus a confession of God's overruling power is extorted from a wicked prophet, to the further confusion of a wicked prince.
entries.4da86aa5cde5bdadf692d5b4cc3f554b1d45b6e7: <div eID="gen3161" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Balaam Again Blesses Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1452.)</title> <div sID="gen3162" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> And Balak said unto him, Come, I pray thee, with me unto another place, from whence thou mayest see them: thou shalt see but the utmost part of them, and shalt not see them all: and curse me them from thence. 14 And he brought him into the field of Zophim, to the top of Pisgah, and built seven altars, and offered a bullock and a ram on <hi type="italic">every</hi> altar. 15 And he said unto Balak, Stand here by thy burnt offering, while I meet <hi type="italic">the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> </hi> yonder. 16 And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> met Balaam, and put a word in his mouth, and said, Go again unto Balak, and say thus. 17 And when he came to him, behold, he stood by his burnt offering, and the princes of Moab with him. And Balak said unto him, What hath the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spoken? 18 And he took up his parable, and said, Rise up, Balak, and hear; hearken unto me, thou son of Zippor: 19 God <hi type="italic">is</hi> not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do <hi type="italic">it?</hi> or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good? 20 Behold, I have received <hi type="italic">commandment</hi> to bless: and he hath blessed; and I cannot reverse it. 21 He hath not beheld iniquity in Jacob, neither hath he seen perverseness in Israel: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> his God <hi type="italic">is</hi> with him, and the shout of a king <hi type="italic">is</hi> among them. 22 God brought them out of Egypt; he hath as it were the strength of an unicorn. 23 Surely <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no enchantment against Jacob, neither <hi type="italic">is there</hi> any divination against Israel: according to this time it shall be said of Jacob and of Israel, What hath God wrought! 24 Behold, the people shall rise up as a great lion, and lift up himself as a young lion: he shall not lie down until he eat <hi type="italic">of</hi> the prey, and drink the blood of the slain. 25 And Balak said unto Balaam, Neither curse them at all, nor bless them at all. 26 But Balaam answered and said unto Balak, Told not I thee, saying, All that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> speaketh, that I must do? 27 And Balak said unto Balaam, Come, I pray thee, I will bring thee unto another place; peradventure it will please God that thou mayest curse me them from thence. 28 And Balak brought Balaam unto the top of Peor, that looketh toward Jeshimon. 29 And Balaam said unto Balak, Build me here seven altars, and prepare me here seven bullocks and seven rams. 30 And Balak did as Balaam had said, and offered a bullock and a ram on <hi type="italic">every</hi> altar. <div eID="gen3162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3163" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Preparation made the second time, as before, for the cursing of Israel. 1. The place is changed, <reference osisRef="Num.23.13">v. 13</reference>. Balak fancied that Balaam, having so full a prospect of the whole camp of Israel, <hi type="italic">from the top of the rocks</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.23.9">v. 9</reference>), was either so enamoured with the beauty of it that he would not curse them or so affrighted with the terror of it that he durst not; and therefore he would bring him to another place, form which he might see only some part of them, which would appear more despicable, and that part at least which would lie in view he hoped he might obtain leave to curse, and so by degrees he should get ground against them, intending, no doubt, if he had gained this point, to make his attack on that part of the camp of Israel which Balaam now had in his eye, and into which he was to throw the fireballs of his curses. See how restless and unwearied the church's enemies are in their malicious attempts to ruin it; they leave no stone unturned, no project untried, to compass it. O that we were as full of contrivance and resolution in prosecuting good designs for the glory of God! 2. The sacrifices are repeated, new altars are built, a bullock and a ram offered on every altar, and Balak attends his sacrifice as closely as ever, <reference osisRef="Num.23.14-Num.23.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. Were we thus earnest to obtain the blessing as Balak was to procure a curse (designedly upon Israel, but really upon himself and his people), we should not grudge the return both of the charge and of the labour of religious exercises. 3. Balaam renews his attendance on God, and God meets him the second time, and puts another word into his mouth, not to reverse the former, but to ratify it, <reference osisRef="Num.23.16-Num.23.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. If God said not to Balaam, <hi type="italic">Seek in vain,</hi> much less will he say so to <hi type="italic">any of the seed of Jacob,</hi> who shall surely find him, not only as Balaam, their instructor and oracle, but their bountiful rewarder. When Balaam returned Balak was impatient to know what message he had: "<hi type="italic">What hath the Lord spoken?</hi> Are there any better tidings yet, any hopes of speeding?" This should be our enquiry when we come to hear the word of God. See <reference osisRef="Jer.23.35">Jer. xxiii. 35</reference>. <div eID="gen3163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3164" type="x-p"/> II. A second conversion of the curse into a blessing by the overruling power of God; and this blessing is both larger and stronger than the former, and quite cuts off all hopes of altering it. Balak having been so forward to ask what the Lord had spoken (<reference osisRef="Num.23.17">v. 17</reference>), Balaam now addresses himself particularly to him (<reference osisRef="Num.23.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">Rise up, Balak, and hear.</hi> It was a message from God that he had to deliver, and it is required of Balak, though a king, that he attend (<hi type="italic">hear</hi> and <hi type="italic">hearken,</hi> with a close application of mind, let not a word slip), and also that he attend with reverence: <hi type="italic">Rise up, and hear.</hi> His successor Eglon, when he was to receive a message from God, <hi type="italic">rose out of his seat,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.3.20">Judg. iii. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen3164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3165" type="x-p"/> 1. Two things Balaam in this discourse informs Balak of, sorely to his grief and disappointment:— <div eID="gen3165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3166" type="x-p"/> (1.) That he had no reason to hope that he should ruin Israel. <div eID="gen3166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3167" type="x-p"/> [1.] It would be to no purpose to attempt to ruin them, and he would deceive himself if he expected it, for three reasons:— <div eID="gen3167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3168" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Because God is unchangeable: <hi type="italic">God is not a man that he should lie,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.23.19">v. 19</reference>. Men change their minds, and therefore break their words; they lie, because they repent. But God does neither. He never changes his mind, and therefore never recalls his promise. Balaam had owned (<reference osisRef="Num.23.8">v. 8</reference>) that he could not alter God's counsel, and thence he infers here that God himself would not alter it; such is the imperfection of man, and such the perfection of God. It is impossible for God to lie, <reference osisRef="Heb.6.18">Heb. vi. 18</reference>. And, when in scripture he is said to <hi type="italic">repent,</hi> it is not meant of any change of his mind (for <hi type="italic">he is in one mind, and who can turn him?</hi>) but only of the change of his way. This is a great truth, that with God there is no <hi type="italic">variableness nor shadow of turning.</hi> Now here, 1. He appeals to Balak himself concerning it: "<hi type="italic">Hath he said, and shall he not do it?</hi> Said it in his own purpose, and shall he not perform it in his providence, according to the counsel of his will? Hath he spoken in his word, in his promise, and shall he not make it good? Can we think otherwise of God than that he is unchangeably one with himself and true to his word? All his decrees are unalterable, and all his promises inviolable." 2. He applies this general truth to the case in hand (<reference osisRef="Num.23.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">He hath blessed and I cannot reverse it,</hi> that is, "I cannot prevail with him to reverse it." Israel were of old a blessed people, a seed that the Lord had blessed; the blessing of Abraham came upon them; they were born under the blessing of the covenant, and born to the blessing of Canaan, and therefore they could not be cursed, unless you could suppose that the God of eternal truth should break his word, and become false to himself and his people. <div eID="gen3168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3169" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Because Israel are at present unblamable: <hi type="italic">he has not beheld iniquity in Jacob,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.23.21">v. 21</reference>. Not but that there was iniquity in Jacob, and God saw it; but, 1. There was not such a degree of iniquity as might provoke God to abandon them and give them up to ruin. As bad as they were, they were not so bad as this. 2. There was no idolatry among them, which is in a particular manner called iniquity and perverseness; we have found nothing of that kind in Israel since the golden calf, and therefore, though they were in other instances very provoking, yet God would not cast them off. Balaam knew that nothing would separate between them and God but sin. While God saw no reigning sin among them, he would send no destroying curse among them; and therefore, as long as they kept in with God, he despaired of ever doing them any mischief. Note, While we keep from sin we keep from harm. Some give another sense of those words; they read it thus: <hi type="italic">He has not beheld wrong offered to Jacob, nor will he see any grievance done to Israel,</hi> that is, "He has not nor will he permit it, or allow it; he will not see Israel injured, but he will right them, and avenge their quarrel." Note, God will not bear to see any injury done to his church and people; for what is done against them he takes as done against himself, and will reckon for it accordingly. <div eID="gen3169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3170" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Because the power of both was irresistible. He shows Balak that there was no contending with them, it was to no purpose to attempt it; for, 1. They had the presence of God with them: "<hi type="italic">The Lord his God is with him</hi> in a particular manner, and not provoked to withdraw from him." 2. They had the joy of that presence, and were always made to triumph in it: <hi type="italic">The shout</hi> or alarm <hi type="italic">of a king is among them.</hi> They shout against their enemies, as sure of victory and success, glorying continually in God as their King and conqueror for them. 3. They had had the experience of the benefit of God's presence with them, and his power engaged for them; for God <hi type="italic">brought them out of Egypt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.23.22">v. 22</reference>. The power which had done that could never be restrained, never resisted; and, having begun so gloriously, he would no doubt finish gloriously. 4. While they had God's presence with them they had the strength of a unicorn, able to make head against all that opposed them. See <reference osisRef="Num.24.8">ch. xxiv. 8</reference>. Such is the strength which the God of Israel gives unto his people. <div eID="gen3170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3171" type="x-p"/> [2.] From all this he infers that it was to no purpose for him to think of doing them a mischief by all the arts he could use, <reference osisRef="Num.23.23">v. 23</reference>. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He owns himself baffled. Surely there is no enchantment against Jacob so as to prevail. The curses of hell can never take place against the blessings of heaven. Not but that attempts of this kind would be made, but they would certainly be fruitless and ineffectual. Some observe that <hi type="italic">Jacob</hi> denotes the church low and afflicted, <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> denotes it prosperous and advanced; but be the church high or low, be her friends few or many, let second causes smile or frown, it comes all to one: no weapon formed against it shall prosper. Note, God easily can, and certainly will, baffle and disappoint all the devices and designs of the powers of darkness against his church, so that they shall not prevail to destroy it. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He foresees that this would be remembered in time to come. <hi type="italic">According to this time,</hi> that is, with reference to this we are now about, it shall be said concerning Jacob and Israel, and said by them, <hi type="italic">What hath God wrought!</hi> What great things hath God done for his people! It shall be said with wonder, joy, and thankfulness, and a challenge to the neighbouring nations to produce any similar instances of the care of their gods for them. Note, The defeating of the designs of the church's enemies ought to be had in everlasting remembrance to the glory of God. <hi type="italic">There is none like unto the God of Jeshurun.</hi> What Balaam says here concerning the pre-eminence of the God of Israel above all the gods of the Gentiles perhaps Moses refers to when he says (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.31">Deut. xxxii. 31</reference>), <hi type="italic">Their rock is not as our rock, even our enemies themselves being judges,</hi> Balaam particularly. Balak therefore has no hopes of ruining Israel. But, <div eID="gen3171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3172" type="x-p"/> (2.) Balaam shows him that he had more reason to fear being ruined by them, for they were likely to make bloody work among his neighbours; and, if he and his country escaped, it was not because he was too great for them to meddle with, but because he fell not within their commission <reference osisRef="Num.23.24">v. 24</reference>. Behold, and tremble; the people that now have lain for some time closely encamped do but repose themselves for a while like a lion couchant, but shortly they <hi type="italic">shall rise up as a great lion,</hi> a lion rampant, that <hi type="italic">shall not lie down till he eat of the prey, and drink the blood of the slain.</hi> This seems to point at the victories he foresaw they would obtain over the Canaanites, that they would never lay down their arms till they had made a complete conquest of the land they had now in view; and, when his neighbour's house was on fire, he had reason to think his own in danger. <div eID="gen3172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3173" type="x-p"/> 2. Now what was the issue of this disappointment? <div eID="gen3173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3174" type="x-p"/> (1.) Balak and Balaam were both of them sick of the cause. [1.] Balak is now willing to have his conjurer silenced. Since he cannot say what he would have him, he wishes him to say nothing: "<hi type="italic">Neither curse them at all nor bless them at all,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.23.25">v. 25</reference>. If thou canst not curse them, I beseech thee not to bless them. If thou canst no assist and encourage my forces, yet do not oppose and dispirit them" Note, God can make those that depart from him weary of the <hi type="italic">multitude of their counsels,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.47.13">Isa. xlvii. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.10">lvii. 10</reference>. [2.] Balaam is still willing to own himself overruled, and appeals to what he had said in the beginning of this enterprise (<reference osisRef="Num.22.38">ch. xxii. 38</reference>): <hi type="italic">All that the Lord speaketh, that I must do,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.23.26">v. 26</reference>. This sows, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> In general, that the way of man is not in himself; there are many devices in man's heart, but God's counsels shall stand. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> In particular, that, as no weapon formed against the church shall prosper, so every tongue that rises against her in judgment God will control and condemn, <reference osisRef="Isa.54.17">Isa. liv. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen3174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3175" type="x-p"/> (2.) Yet they resolve to make another attempt. They think it scorn to be baffled, and therefore pursue the design, though it be only to their further confusion. And now the third time, [1.] They change the place. Balak is at last convinced that it is not Balaam's fault, on whom, before, he had laid the blame, but that really he was under a divine check, and therefore now he hopes to bring him to a place whence God might at least permit him to curse them, <reference osisRef="Num.23.27">v. 27</reference>. Probably he and Balaam were the more encouraged thus to repeat their attempt because God had the second time allowed Balaam to go, though he had forbidden him the first time. Since by repeated trials they had carried that point, they hope in like manner to carry this. Thus because sinners are borne with, and sentence against their evil works is not executed speedily, their hearts are the more fully set in them to do evil. The place to which Balak now took Balaam was the top of Peor, the most eminent high place in all his country, where, it is probable, Baal was worshipped, and it was thence called <hi type="italic">Baal-peor.</hi> He chose this place with a hope, either, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That it being the residence (as he fancied) of Baal, the god of Moab, Jehovah the God of Israel would not, or could not, come hither to hinder the operation; or, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That, it being a place acceptable to his god, it would be so to the Lord, and there he would be brought into a good humour. Such idle conceits have foolish men of God, and so vain are their imaginations concerning him. Thus the Syrians fancied the Lord to be God of the hills, but not of the valleys (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.28">1 Kings xx. 28</reference>), as if he were more powerful in one place than he is in every place. [2.] They repeat their sacrifice, seven bullocks and seven rams, upon seven altars, <reference osisRef="Num.23.29-Num.23.30">v. 29, 30</reference>. Thus do they persevere in their expensive oblations, though they had no promise on which to build their hopes of speeding. Let not us therefore, who have a promise that the vision at the end shall speak and not lie, be discouraged by delays, but continue instant in prayer, and not faint, <reference osisRef="Luke.18.1">Luke xviii. 1</reference>.  <chapter eID="Num.23"/> <div eID="gen3175" type="x-p"/>

entries.b85985553beb64a65344fe283bed09992fbd1708: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1505"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 23</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Num.23.1-Num.23.30">Nu 23:1-30</reference>. Balak's Sacrifices.</title> <div sID="gen2015" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1505"/><hi type="bold">1. Balaam said unto Balak, Build me here seven altars--</hi>Balak, being a heathen, would naturally suppose these altars were erected in honor of Baal, the patron deity of his country. It is evident, from <reference osisRef="Num.23.4">Nu 23:4</reference> that they were prepared for the worship of the true God; although in choosing the high places of Baal as their site and rearing a number of altars (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.22">2Ki 18:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.17.8">Is 17:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.11.13">Jr 11:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.8.11">Ho 8:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.10.1">10:1</reference>), instead of one only, as God had appointed, Balaam blended his own superstitions with the divine worship. The heathen, both in ancient and modern times, attached a mysterious virtue to the number seven; and Balaam, in ordering the preparation of so many altars, designed to mystify and delude the king. <div eID="gen2015" type="x-p"/>
entries.207e2eed3f758629a8a0d9339c39e811940e8d7f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1506"/><div sID="gen2016" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1506"/><hi type="bold">3. Stand by thy burnt offering--</hi>as one in expectation of an important favor.<div eID="gen2016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2017" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">peradventure the Lord will come to meet me: and whatsoever he showeth me--</hi>that is, makes known to me by word or sign.<div eID="gen2017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2018" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he went to an high place--</hi>apart by himself, where he might practise rites and ceremonies, with a view to obtain a response of the oracle. <div eID="gen2018" type="x-p"/>
entries.2921a16768cc7ef9f805649be9b9e2b552ecd7c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1507"/><div sID="gen2019" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1507"/><hi type="bold">4-6. God met Balaam--</hi>not in compliance with his incantations, but to frustrate his wicked designs and compel him, contrary to his desires and interests, to pronounce the following benediction [Nu 23:8-10]. <div eID="gen2019" type="x-p"/>
entries.d6e95ab8666a9372cff397979e8d5043e1aa5a17: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1508"/><div sID="gen2020" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1508"/><hi type="bold">7. took up his parable--</hi>that is, spoke under the influence of inspiration, and in the highly poetical, figurative, and oracular style of a prophet.<div eID="gen2020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2021" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brought me from Aram--</hi>This word joined with "the mountains of the East," denotes the upper portion of Mesopotamia, lying on the east of Moab. The East enjoyed an infamous notoriety for magicians and soothsayers (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.6">Is 2:6</reference>). <div eID="gen2021" type="x-p"/>
entries.f61a35c39c59cee225d1a59190dd510a930db02f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1509"/><div sID="gen2022" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1509"/><hi type="bold">8. How shall I curse, whom God hath not cursed?--</hi>A divine blessing has been pronounced over the posterity of Jacob; and therefore, whatever prodigies can be achieved by my charms, all magical skill, all human power, is utterly impotent to counteract the decree of God. <div eID="gen2022" type="x-p"/>
entries.c62c2018e11569032716fa937bdcb999a63ef2ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1510"/><div sID="gen2023" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1510"/><hi type="bold">9. from the top--</hi>literally, "a bare place" on the rocks, to which Balak had taken him, for it was deemed necessary to see the people who were to be devoted to destruction. But that commanding prospect could contribute nothing to the accomplishment of the king's object, for the destiny of Israel was to be a distinct, peculiar people, separated from the rest of the nations in government, religion, customs, and divine protection (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.28">De 33:28</reference>). So that although I might be able to gratify your wishes against other people, I can do nothing against them (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.5">Ex 19:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.20.24">Le 20:24</reference>). <div eID="gen2023" type="x-p"/>
entries.b3af3d148ca56f86668eeeb719c77110febd61eb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1511"/><div sID="gen2024" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1511"/><hi type="bold">10. Who can count the dust of Jacob?--</hi>an Oriental hyperbole for a very populous nation, as Jacob's posterity was promised to be (<reference osisRef="Gen.13.16">Ge 13:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.28.14">28:14</reference>).<div eID="gen2024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2025" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the number of the fourth part of Israel--</hi>that is, the camp consisted of four divisions; every one of these parts was formidable in numbers.<div eID="gen2025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2026" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Let me die the death of the righteous--</hi>Hebrew, "of Jeshurun"; or, the Israelites. The meaning is: they are a people happy, above all others, not only in life, but at death, from their knowledge of the true God, and their hope through His grace. Balaam is a representative of a large class in the world, who express a wish for the blessedness which Christ has promised to His people but are averse to imitate the mind that was in Him. <div eID="gen2026" type="x-p"/>
entries.79c24b5721028b67c0d638333762dda4fc9c4849: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1512"/><div sID="gen2027" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1512"/><hi type="bold">13-15. Come, ... with me unto another place, from whence thou mayest see them--</hi>Surprised and disappointed at this unexpected eulogy on Israel, Balak hoped that, if seen from a different point of observation, the prophet would give utterance to different feelings; and so, having made the same solemn preparations, Balaam retired, as before, to wait the divine afflatus. <div eID="gen2027" type="x-p"/>
entries.716c967a0a167d0f6e4a0820da1f96c1189fba66: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1514"/><div sID="gen2029" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1514"/><hi type="bold">18-19. Rise up--</hi>As Balak was already standing (<reference osisRef="Num.23.17">Nu 23:17</reference>), this expression is equivalent to "now attend to me." The counsels and promises of God respecting Israel are unchangeable; and no attempt to prevail on Him to reverse them will succeed, as they may with a man. <div eID="gen2029" type="x-p"/>
entries.d8c3e0af5c2129a63a594b4b227dafecb5d969e3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1515"/><div sID="gen2030" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1515"/><hi type="bold">21. He hath not beheld iniquity in Jacob--</hi>Many sins were observed and punished in this people. But no such universal and hopeless apostasy had as yet appeared, to induce God to abandon or destroy them.<div eID="gen2030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2031" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord his God is with him--</hi>has a favor for them.<div eID="gen2031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2032" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the shout of a king is among them--</hi>such joyful acclamations as of a people rejoicing in the presence of a victorious prince. <div eID="gen2032" type="x-p"/>
entries.83910060384023806a8109c9f74fe42c539d42f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1516"/><div sID="gen2033" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1516"/><hi type="bold">22. he hath as it were the strength of an unicorn--</hi>Israel is not as they were at the Exodus, a horde of poor, feeble, spiritless people, but powerful and invincible as a reem--that is, a rhinoceros (<reference osisRef="Job.39.9">Job 39:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.22.21">Psa 22:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.92.10">92:10</reference>). <div eID="gen2033" type="x-p"/>
entries.23ac08c68401a29b333b9aa28c705156f48b3e14: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1517"/><div sID="gen2034" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1517"/><hi type="bold">23. Surely there is no enchantment against Jacob--</hi>No art can ever prevail against a people who are under the shield of Omnipotence, and for whom miracles have been and yet shall be performed, which will be a theme of admiration in succeeding ages. <div eID="gen2034" type="x-p"/>
entries.60937669c85f77e029df4b539ef5d1d2425d2d45: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1518"/><div sID="gen2035" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1518"/><hi type="bold">26. All that the Lord speaketh, that I must do--</hi>a remarkable confession that he was divinely constrained to give utterances different from what it was his purpose and inclination to do. <div eID="gen2035" type="x-p"/>
entries.6569cc1a1b80b5063c342118059b6042c1801461: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1519"/><div sID="gen2036" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1519"/><hi type="bold">28. Balak brought Balaam unto the top of Peor--</hi>or, Beth-peor (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.29">De 3:29</reference>), the eminence on which a temple of Baal stood.<div eID="gen2036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2037" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that looketh toward Jeshimon--</hi>the desert tract in the south of Palestine, on both sides of the Dead Sea. <chapter eID="Num.23"/>

entries.37452b859cf9cf92efcbf39a9062905ac4eeb24f: <div eID="gen5951" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen5952" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5953" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5953" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5952" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5954" type="x-p"/> Being arrived at the high places of Baal, (<reference osisRef="Num.22.41">Num 22:41</reference>), Balaam orders Balak to build seven altars, and prepare oxen and rams for sacrifice, <reference osisRef="Num.23.1">Num 23:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.23.2">Num 23:2</reference>. Balaam inquires of the Lord, receives an answer, with which he returns to Balak, <reference osisRef="Num.23.3-Num.23.10">Num 23:3-10</reference>. Balak, finding that this was a prediction of the prosperity of the Israelites, is greatly troubled, <reference osisRef="Num.23.11">Num 23:11</reference>. Balaam excuses himself, <reference osisRef="Num.23.12">Num 23:12</reference>. He brings him to another place, where he might see only a part of Israel, and repeats his sacrifices, <reference osisRef="Num.23.13">Num 23:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.23.14">Num 23:14</reference>. Balaam again consults the Lord, <reference osisRef="Num.23.15-Num.23.17">Num 23:15-17</reference>. Returns with his answer, and again predicts the glory of Israel, <reference osisRef="Num.23.18-Num.23.24">Num 23:18-24</reference>. Balak is angry, <reference osisRef="Num.23.25">Num 23:25</reference>; and Balaam again excuses himself. Balak proposes another trial, takes him to another place, and repeats the same sacrifices, <reference osisRef="Num.23.26-Num.23.30">Num 23:26-30</reference>. <div eID="gen5954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5955" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen5955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5956" type="x-p"/> Build me here seven altars, etc. - The oxen and the rams were such as the Mosaic law had ordered to be offered to God in sacrifice; the building of seven altars was not commanded. Some think that these seven altars were built to the seven planets: this is most gratuitously said; of it there is no proof whatever; it is mere trifling, even with conjecture. As seven was a number of perfection, Balaam chose it on this occasion, because he intended to offer a grand sacrifice, and to offer a bullock and a ram upon each of the altars; the whole to be made a burnt-offering at the same time. And as he intended to offer seven bullocks and seven rams at the same time, it could not be conveniently done on one altar, therefore he ordered seven to be built. We need go no farther to find out his reasons.
entries.1dfb5203e1e3a6cdf13fb9fc7684fbad14303fb7: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen5956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5957" type="x-p"/> Stand by thy burnt-offering - We have already seen that blessing and cursing in this way were considered as religious rites, and therefore must be always preceded by sacrifice. See this exemplified in the case of Isaac, before he blessed Jacob and Esau, Genesis 27 (note), and the notes there. The venison that was brought to Isaac, of which he did eat, was properly the preparatory sacrifice.
entries.d5770a53916c6b074d013f60ec0862ee96681ed1: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen5957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5958" type="x-p"/> And he took up his parable - משלו meshalo, see on <reference osisRef="Num.21.27">Num 21:27</reference> (note). All these oracular speeches of Balaam are in hemistich metre in the original. They are highly dignified, and may be considered as immediate poetic productions of the Spirit of God; for it is expressly said, <reference osisRef="Num.23.5">Num 23:5</reference>, that God put the word in Balaam's mouth, and that the Spirit of God came upon him, <reference osisRef="Num.24.2">Num 24:2</reference>.
entries.e34a2beb3cfcd8a2b616e105b01f8ebc20682417: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen5958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5959" type="x-p"/> How shall I curse, whom God hath not cursed? - It was granted on all hands that no incantations nor imprecations could avail, unless God concurred and ratified them. From God's communication to Balaam he saw that God was determined to bless and defend Israel, and therefore all endeavors to injure them must be in vain.
entries.f98b80d05d5fdb8a87ad5d8e072eeab02f879261: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen5959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5960" type="x-p"/> From the top of the rocks I see him - That is, from the high places of Baal where he went, <reference osisRef="Num.22.41">Num 22:41</reference>, that he might the more advantageously see the whole camp of Israel. <div eID="gen5960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5961" type="x-p"/> The people shall dwell alone - They shall ever be preserved as a distinct nation. This prophecy has been literally fulfilled through a period of 3300 years to the present day. This is truly astonishing.
entries.268bf55664f1dce1009bcf729642f6cadbcec2a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen5961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5962" type="x-p"/> Let me die the death of the righteous - Probably Balaam had some presentiment that he should be taken off by a premature death, and therefore he lodges this petition against it. The death of the righteous in those times implied being gathered to one's fathers in a good old age, having seen his children, and children's children; and to this, probably, the latter part of this petition applies: And let my last end be like his, (ותהי אחריתי כמהו uthehi acharithi chamohu, And let my Posterity be like his). It has been generally supposed that Balaam is here praying for a happy death, such as true Christians die who die in the Lord; and in this way his words are generally applied; but I am satisfied this is not their meaning. The prayer, however, understood in the common way, is a good one, and may be offered to God profitably. A righteous man is one who is saved from his sins, who is justified and sanctified through the blood of the covenant, and who lives, not only an innocent, but also a holy and useful life. He who would die well should live well; for a bad death must be the issue of a bad life.
entries.f8f7eb1fbf368f4d69ed2f40c9cfca8aa1f7d4ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen5962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5963" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt see but the utmost part of them - Balak thought that the sight of such an immense camp had intimidated Balaam, and this he might gather from what he said in the tenth verse: Who can count the dust of Jacob, etc.; he thought therefore that he might get Balaam to curse them in detached parties, till the whole camp should be devoted to destruction by successive execrations.
entries.019fb7c0b6d885b915f73ce831fdc38f044f79d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen5963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5964" type="x-p"/> What hath the Lord spoken? - Balak himself now understood that Balaam was wholly under the influence of Jehovah, and would say nothing but what God commanded him; but not knowing Jehovah as Balaam did, he hoped that he might be induced to change his mind, and curse a people whom he had hitherto determined to bless.
entries.f292fba27e1ee6a2f904419b228061a7042b22cc: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen5964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5965" type="x-p"/> God is not a man, that he should lie - This seems to be spoken to correct the foregoing supposition of Balak that God could change his mind. Even the heathen would not allow that their supreme god could be caught in a falsity. Hence Aeschylus, in Prometh. vinct. 1068: - Ψευδηγορειν γαρ ουκ επισταται στομα Το Διον, αλλα παν επος τελει. "The mouth of Jove knows not to frame a lie; <div eID="gen5965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5966" type="x-p"/> But every word finds full accomplishment."
entries.fca180395dbd08a9a04ca40ede68594bce01a571: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen5966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5967" type="x-p"/> He hath not beheld iniquity in Jacob, neither hath he seen perverseness in Israel - This is a difficult passage; for if we take the words as spoken of the people Israel, as their iniquity and their perverseness were almost unparalleled, such words cannot be spoken of them with strict truth. If we consider them as spoken of the patriarch Jacob and Israel, or of Jacob after he became Israel, they are most strictly true, as after that time a more unblemished and noble character (Abraham excepted) is not to be found in the page of history, whether sacred or profane; and for his sake, and for the sake of his father Isaac, and his grandfather Abraham, God is ever represented as favoring, blessing, and sparing a rebellious and undeserving people; see the note on <reference osisRef="Gen.49.33">Gen 49:33</reference>. In this way, I think, this difficult text may be safely understood. <div eID="gen5967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5968" type="x-p"/> There is another way in which the words may be interpreted, which will give a good sense. און aven not only signifies iniquity, but most frequently trouble, labor, distress, and affliction; and these indeed are its ideal meanings, and iniquity is only an accommodated or metaphorical one, because of the pain, distress, etc., produced by sin. עמל amal, translated here perverseness, occurs often in Scripture, but is never translated perverseness except in this place. It signifies simply labor, especially that which is of an afflictive or oppressive kind. The words may therefore be considered as implying that God will not suffer the people either to be exterminated by the sword, or to be brought under a yoke of slavery. Either of these methods of interpretation gives a good sense, but our common version gives none. <div eID="gen5968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5969" type="x-p"/> Dr. Kennicott contends for the reading of the Samaritan, which, instead of לא הביט lo hibbit, he hath not seen, has לא אבט lo abbit, I do not see, I do not discover any thing among them on which I could ground my curse. But the sense above given is to be preferred.
entries.fdc7381dc76ddcc6fee241a331498b893b51fcbe: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen5969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5970" type="x-p"/> The strength of a unicorn - ראם reem and ראים reim. It is generally allowed that there is no such beast in nature as the unicorn; i. e., a creature of the horse kind, with one long rich curled horn in the forehead. The creature painted from fancy is represented as one of the supporters of the royal arms of Great Britain. It is difficult to say what kind of beast is intended by the original word. The Septuagint translate the word μονοκερως, the unicorn, or one-horned animal; the Vulgate, sometimes, unicornus; and in the text rhinocerotis, by which the rhinoceros, a creature which has its name from the horn on its nose, is supposed to be meant. That no single-horned animal can be intended by the reem of Moses, is sufficiently evident from this, that Moses, speaking of Joseph, says, "he has the Horns of A unicorn," or reem, where the horns are spoken of in the plural, the animal in the singular. The creature referred to is either the rhinoceros, some varieties of which have two horns on the nose, or the wild bull, urus, or buffalo; though some think the beast intended is a species of goat; but the rhinoceros seems the most likely. There is literally a monoceros, or unicorn, with one large curled ivory horn growing horizontally out of his snout; but this is not a land animal, it is the modiodan or nurwal, a marine animal of the whale kind, a horn of which is now before me, measuring seven feet four inches; but I believe the rhinoceros is that intended by the sacred writers.
entries.eb5a0fb887800946427955167e51e83a8673c70b: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen5970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5971" type="x-p"/> There is no enchantment, etc. - Because God has determined to save them, therefore no enchantment can prevail against them. <div eID="gen5971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5972" type="x-p"/> According to this time, etc. - I think this clause should be read thus: "As at this time it shall be told to Jacob and to Israel what God worketh;" i. e., this people shall always have prophetic information of what God is about to work. And indeed, they are the only people under heaven who ever had this privilege. When God himself designed to punish them because of their sins, he always forewarned them by the prophets; and also took care to apprise them of all the plots of their enemies against them.
entries.887f276dd3d7a24274fbdbfd7e80bb94e5e7a8ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen5972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5973" type="x-p"/> Behold, the people shall rise up as a great lion - לביא labi, the great, mighty, or old lion, the king of the forest, who is feared and respected by all the other beasts of the field; so shall Israel be the subduer and possessor of the whole land of Canaan. And as a young lion, ארי ari from ארה arah, to tear off, the predatory lion, or the lion in the act of seizing and tearing his prey; - the nations against whom the Israelites are now going shall be no more able to defend themselves against their attacks, than the feeblest beasts of the forest are against the attacks of the strong lion.
entries.4c0eb1021e8d1422ce01059a6c7e22bf5d4a4179: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen5973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5974" type="x-p"/> Unto the top of Peor - Probably the place where the famous Baal-peor had his chief temple. He appears to have been the Priapus of the Moabites, and to have been worshipped with the same obscene and abominable rites.  <chapter eID="Num.23"/> <div eID="gen5974" type="x-p"/>

entries.e5b6d4647e72ebe78cbbe3806ac383279e5c06a0: Num 23:1-2 <div eID="gen1928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1929" type="x-p"/> Balaam’s First Words. - Num 23:1-3. <hi type="italic">Preparations</hi> for the first act, which was performed at Bamoth-baal. At Balaam’s command Balak built seven altars, and then selected seven bullocks and seven rams, which they immediately sacrificed, namely, one bullock and one ram upon each altar. The nations of antiquity generally accompanied all their more important undertakings with sacrifices, to make sure of the protection and help of the gods; but this was especially the case with their ceremonies of adjuration. According to <hi type="italic">Diod. Sic.</hi> ii. 29, the Chaldeans sought to avert calamity and secure prosperity by sacrifices and adjurations. The same thing is also related of other nations (see Hengstenberg, Balaam, p. 392). Accordingly, Balaam also did everything that appeared necessary, according to his own religious notions, to ensure the success of Balak’s undertaking, and bring about the desired result. The erection of <hi type="italic">seven</hi> altars, and the sacrifice of <hi type="italic">seven</hi> animals of each kind, are to be explained from the sacredness acquired by this number, through the creation of the world in seven days, as being the stamp of work that was well-pleasing to God. The sacrifices were burnt-offerings, and were offered by themselves to Jehovah, whom Balaam acknowledged as his God.
entries.614325476193dfe840cc200b9ecfd7c951fc3f46: Num 23:3-4 <div eID="gen1929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1930" type="x-p"/> After the offering of the sacrifices, Balaam directed the king to stand by his burnt-offering, i.e., by the sacrifices that had been offered for him upon the seven altars, that he might go out for auguries. The meaning of the words, “<hi type="italic">I will go, peradventure Jehovah will come to meet me,</hi>” is apparent from Num 24:1 : and “<hi type="italic">he went no more to meet with the auguries</hi>” (נחשׁים, see at <reference osisRef="Lev.19.26">Lev 19:26</reference>). Balaam went out to look for a manifestation of Jehovah in the significant phenomena of nature. The word which Jehovah should show to him, he would report to Balak. We have here what is just as characteristic in relation to Balaam’s religious stand-point, as it is significant in its bearing upon the genuine historical character of the narrative, namely, an admixture of the religious ideas of both the Israelites and the heathen, inasmuch as Balaam hoped to receive or discover, in the phenomena of nature, a revelation from Jehovah. Because heathenism had no “sure word of prophecy,” it sought to discover the will and counsel of God, which are displayed in the events of human history, through various signs that were discernible in natural phenomena, or, as <hi type="italic">Chryssipus</hi> the Stoic expresses it in <hi type="italic">Cicero de divin.</hi> ii. 63, “<hi type="italic">Signa quae a Diis hominibus portendantur</hi>.”<note placement="foot">See the remarks of Nägelsbach and Hartung on the nature of the heathen auspices, in Hengstenberg’s Balaam and his Prophecies (pp. 396-7). Hartung observes, for example: “As the gods did not live outside the world, or separated from it, but the things of time and space were filled with their essence, it followed, as a matter of course, that the signs of their presence were sought and seen in all the visible and audible occurrences of nature, whether animate or inanimate. Hence all the phenomena which affected the senses, either in the elements or in the various creatures, whether sounds or movements, natural productions or events, of a mechanical or physical, or voluntary or involuntary kind, might serve as the media of revelation.” And again (p. 397): “The sign in itself is useless, if it be not observed. It was therefore necessary that man and God should come to meet one another, and that the sign should not merely be given, but should also be received.”</note> <div eID="gen1930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1931" type="x-p"/> To look for a word of Jehovah in this way, Balaam betook himself to a “bald height.” This is the only meaning of שׁפי, from שׁפה, to rub, to scrape, to make bare, which is supported by the usage of the language; it is also in perfect harmony with the context, as the heathen augurs were always accustomed to select elevated places for their auspices, with an extensive prospect, especially the towering and barren summits of mountains that were rarely visited by men (see Hengstenberg<hi type="italic">, ut sup</hi>.). <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, however, proposes the meaning “alone,” or “to spy,” for which there is not the slightest grammatical foundation.
entries.c9f7446946a799e019c83d56d7016cc3cad41e18: Num 23:7-10 <div eID="gen1932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1933" type="x-p"/> Balaam’s <hi type="italic">first</hi> saying. - Having come back to the burnt-offering, Balaam commenced his utterance before the king and the assembled princes. משׁל, lit., a simile, then a proverb, because the latter consists of comparisons and figures, and lastly a sentence or saying. The application of this term to the announcements made by Balaam (Num 23:7, Num 23:18, Num 24:3, Num 24:15, Num 24:20), whereas it is never used of the prophecies of the true prophets of Jehovah, but only of certain songs and similes inserted in them (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.14.4">Isa 14:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.2">Eze 17:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.3">Eze 24:3</reference>; Mic 2:4), is to be accounted for not merely from the poetic form of Balaam’s utterances, the predominance of poetical imagery, the sustained parallelism, the construction of the whole discourse in brief pointed sentences, and other peculiarities of poetic language (e.g., בּנו, Num 24:3, Num 24:15), but it points at the same time to the difference which actually exists between these utterances and the predictions of the true prophets. The latter are orations addressed to the congregation, which deduce from the general and peculiar relation of Israel to the Lord and to His law, the conduct of the Lord towards His people either in their own or in future times, proclaiming judgment upon the ungodly and salvation to the righteous. “Balaam’s mental eye,” on the contrary, as Hengstenberg correctly observes, “was simply fixed upon what he saw; and this he reproduced without any regard to the impression that it was intended to make upon those who heard it.” But the very first utterance was of such a character as to deprive Balak of all hope that his wishes would be fulfilled.  Num 23:7 <div eID="gen1933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1934" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Balak, the king of Moab, fetches me from Aram, from the mountains of the East,</hi>” i.e., of Mesopotamia, which was described, as far back as <reference osisRef="Gen.29.1">Gen 29:1</reference>, as the land of the sons of the East (cf. Num 22:5). Balaam mentions the mountains of his home in contradistinction to the mountains of the land of the Moabites upon which he was then standing. “<hi type="italic">Come, curse me Jacob, and come threaten Israel</hi>.” Balak had sent for him for this purpose (see Num 22:11, Num 22:17). זעמה, for זעמה, imperative (see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §228, <hi type="italic">b</hi>.). זעם, to be angry, here to give utterance to the wrath of God, synonymous with נקב or קבב, to curse. <hi type="italic">Jacob:</hi> a poetical name for the nation, equivalent to <hi type="italic">Israel</hi>.
entries.9c73b3b70ce4c29abdf3b511183135e4abbe5401: Num 23:11-17 <div eID="gen1936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1937" type="x-p"/> Balak reproached Balaam for this utterance, which announced blessings to the Israelites instead of curses. But he met his reproaches with the remark, that he was bound by the command of Jehovah. The infinitive absolute, בּרך, after the finite verb, expresses the fact that Balaam had continued to give utterance to nothing but blessings. לדבּר שׁמר, to observe to speak; שׁמר, to notice carefully, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.5.1">Deu 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.5.29">Deu 5:29</reference>, etc. But Balak thought that the reason might be found in the unfavourable locality; he therefore led the seer to “<hi type="italic">the field of the watchers, upon the top of Pisgah</hi>,” whence he could see the whole of the people of Israel. The words וגו תּראנּוּ אשׁר (Num 23:13) are to be rendered, “<hi type="italic">whence thou wilt see it</hi> (Israel); <hi type="italic">thou seest only the end of it, but not the whole of it</hi>” (sc., here upon Bamoth-baal). This is required by a comparison of the verse before us with Num 22:41, where it is most unquestionably stated, that upon the top of Bamoth-baal Balaam only saw “the end of the people.” For this reason Balak regarded that place as unfavourable, and wished to lead the seer to a place from which he could see the people, without any limitation whatever. Consequently, notwithstanding the omission of כּי (for), the words קצהוּ אפס can only be intended to assign the reason why Balak supposed the first utterances of Balaam to have been unfavourable. קצהוּ = העם קצה, the end of the people (Num 22:41), cannot possibly signify the whole nation, or, as <hi type="italic">Marck, de Geer, Gesenius,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Kurtz</hi> suppose, “the people from one end to the other,” in which case העם קצה (the end of the people) would signify the very opposite of קצהוּ (the end of it); for העם קצה is not interchangeable, or to be identified, with מקּצה כּל־העם (<reference osisRef="Gen.19.4">Gen 19:4</reference>), “the whole people, from the end or extremity of it,” or from its last man; in other words, “to the very last man.” Still less does העם קצה אפס signify “the uttermost end of the whole people, the end of the entire people,” notwithstanding the fact that <hi type="italic">Kurtz</hi> regards the expression, “the end of the end of the people,” as an intolerable tautology. קבנו, imperative with <hi type="italic">nun</hi> <hi type="italic">epenth</hi>., from קבב. The “field of the watchers,” or “spies (<hi type="italic">zophim</hi>), upon the top of <hi type="italic">Pisgah</hi>,” corresponds, no doubt, to “the field of Moab, upon the top of <hi type="italic">Pisgah</hi>,” on the west of Heshbon (see at Num 21:20). Mount <hi type="italic">Nebo</hi>, from which Moses surveyed the land of Canaan in all its length and breadth, was one summit, and possibly <hi type="italic">the</hi> summit of Pisgah (see <reference osisRef="Deut.3.27">Deu 3:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.34.1">Deu 34:1</reference>). The field of the spies was very probably a tract of table-land upon Nebo; and so called either because watchers were stationed there in times of disturbance, to keep a look-out all round, or possibly because it was a place where augurs made their observations of the heavens and of birds (<hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>). The locality has not been thoroughly explored by travellers; but from the spot alluded to, it must have been possible to overlook a very large portion of the <hi type="italic">Arboth Moab</hi>. Still farther to the north, and nearer to the camp of the Israelites in these Arboth, was the summit of <hi type="italic">Peor</hi>, to which Balak afterwards conducted Balaam (Num 23:28), and where he not only saw the whole of the people, but could see distinctly the camps of the different tribes (Num 24:2).
entries.c5a3bf1ba47d517c0f475c087b5df7b1bdf0500b: Num 23:19 <div eID="gen1939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1940" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">God is not a man, that He should lie; nor a son of man, that He should repent: hath He said, and should He not do it? and spoken, and should not carry it out?</hi>”
entries.a38fa3a29d7b4f37ff23759d9c65857e8bc37f55: Num 23:20 <div eID="gen1940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1941" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Behold, I have received to bless: and He hath blessed; and I cannot turn it</hi>.” Balaam meets Balak’s expectation that he will take back the blessing that he has uttered, with the declaration, that God does not alter His purposes like changeable and fickle men, but keeps His word unalterably, and carries it into execution. The unchangeableness of the divine purposes is a necessary consequence of the unchangeableness of the divine nature. With regard to His own counsels, God repents of nothing; but this does not prevent the repentance of God, understood as an anthropopathic expression, denoting the pain experienced by the love of God, on account of the destruction of its creatures (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.6.6">Gen 6:6</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Exod.32.14">Exo 32:14</reference>). The ה before הוּא Num 23:19) is the interrogative ה (see <hi type="italic">Ges. </hi>§100, 4). The two clauses of <hi type="italic">Num 23:19</hi>, “Hath He spoken,” etc., taken by themselves, are no doubt of universal application; but taken in connection with the context, they relate specially to what God had spoken through Balaam, in his first utterance with reference to Israel, as we may see from the more precise explanation in Num 23:20, “Behold, I have received to bless’ (לקח, taken, accepted), etc. השׁיב, to lead back, to make a thing retrograde (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.13">Isa 43:13</reference>). Samuel afterwards refused Saul’s request in these words of Balaam (<hi type="italic">Num 23:19</hi>), when he entreated him to revoke his rejection on the part of God (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.29">1Sa 15:29</reference>).
entries.c35f2c8befa547156ac9f3d18d7b8ce8e4896d60: Num 23:21 <div eID="gen1941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1942" type="x-p"/> After this decided reversal of Balak’s expectations, Balaam carried out still more fully the blessing which had been only briefly indicated in his first utterance. “<hi type="italic">He beholds not wickedness in Jacob, and sees not suffering in Israel: Jehovah his God is with him, and the shout</hi> (jubilation) <hi type="italic">of a king in the midst of him</hi>.” The subject in the first sentence is God (see <reference osisRef="Hab.1.3">Hab 1:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hab.1.13">Hab 1:13</reference>). God sees not און, worthlessness, wickedness, and עמל, tribulation, misery, as the consequence of sin, and therefore discovers no reason for cursing the nation. That this applied to the people solely by virtue of their calling as the holy nation of Jehovah, and consequently that there is no denial of the sin of individuals, is evident from the second hemistich, which expresses the thought of the first in a positive form: so that the words, “Jehovah his God is with him,” correspond to the words, “He beholds not wickedness;” and “the shout of a king in the midst of it,” to His not seeing suffering. Israel therefore rejoiced in the blessing of God only so long as it remained faithful to the idea of its divine calling, and continued in covenant fellowship with the Lord. So long the power of the world could do it no harm. The “shout of a king” in Israel is the rejoicing of Israel at the fact that Jehovah dwells and rules as King in the midst of it (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.15.18">Exo 15:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.33.5">Deu 33:5</reference>). Jehovah had manifested Himself as King, by leading them out of Egypt.
entries.3fa6e4c207793b3e17971a08ee0b5a01601fd00b: Num 23:22 <div eID="gen1942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1943" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">God brings them out of Egypt; his strength is like that of a buffalo</hi>.” אל is God as the strong, or mighty one. The participle מוציאם is not used for the preterite, but designates the leading out as still going on, and lasting till the introduction into Canaan.
